newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan court adjourns budget petition.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan court adjourns budget petition.

text.p: A Kenyan high court on Friday adjourned until Monday the hearing of an opposition petition seeking to nullify the country's 1997/98 budget on grounds that it was not read audibly.
High court Judge Moijo ole Keiwua adjourned the case after government lawyers finished submissions urging the court to dismiss the case.
Kenya's National Assembly passed the budget on Thursday, side-stepping an opposition boycott and the legal challenge.
The budget was approved with only members of parliament from the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) and one opposition MP in the chamber, the Daily Nation and East African Standard said.
Opposition MPs have boycotted budget debates after disrupting Mudavadi's budget speech on June 19 to back demands for sweeping constitutional reforms before elections due this year.

Britain's minister of state for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs Tony Lloyd said on Friday Kenya's government had "some way to go" to demonstrate its democratic credentials and urged politicians to cool down before elections later this year.
"We are calling on the opposition and government politicians to cool the temperature and to make sure the election is conducted in a non-violent atmosphere," said Lloyd.

"We are saying to the government that they have some way to go to demonstrate that the principles a democratic election are held under are actually there," Lloyd told a news conference at the end of a two-day trip.
Lloyd declined to specify how the Kenya African National Union (KANU) government fell short over elections, but said voters and candidates should be free to express their views.
Lloyd met President Daniel arap Moi, opposition and church leaders during his trip, part of a visit to South Africa, Kenya and Uganda.
In the hearing, state lawyer Nancy Baraza cited parliament's immunity from prosecution and urged the court to dismiss the case which many legal analysts say has little chance of success.
"Even if there was a judicial review it would have to exclude parliament," Baraza told the court.
Opposition Muturi Kigani is expected to make submissions on Monday urging the court to nullify the budget.

The budget was delivered under chaotic conditions as members of parliament tried to disrupt the speech to press demands for constitutional reforms. They later traded blows with KANU MPs in full view of Moi.
Moi, who must call presidential and parliamentary elections later this year, has ruled out constitutional reforms in this east African nation before the polls.
Earlier this week Moi censured the opposition for taking the budget wrangle to court, saying parliament was the country's supreme legal body and as such could not be overruled by a court.
The opposition challenged the legality of the budget in the courts on the grounds that Mudavadi failed to read it audibly and that Speaker Francis ole Kaparo failed to ensure quiet in the chamber.

In another pro-reform move Kenneth Matiba, chairman of the opposition FORD-Asili party, said he would not register as a voter and called on his supporters to boycott the elections, newspapers and an aide to Matiba said.
Matiba came second to Moi in Kenya's landmark multi-party elections in 1992 which the opposition says were unfair because of the pro-government constitution and electoral rules.
Matiba is the first prominent opposition leader to publicly back a boycott of this year's polls, whose dates have not been announced by Moi.
